claims.text: Rapid quenching under several GPa immediately after melt homogenization will improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
The same high-pressure quenching treatment will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
High-pressure processing in the several-GPa range is experimentally implementable for high-entropy alloys.
High pressure increases atomic packing density during the liquid-to-solid transition.
High pressure reduces atomic mobility or diffusivity during cooling.
Increased packing density and reduced atomic mobility suppress crystalline nucleation and growth.
High pressure decreases the free volume available in the melt.
Reduced melt free volume retards atomic diffusion.
Retarded atomic diffusion slows the kinetics of crystalline nucleation.
Suppression of crystallization lowers the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
The pressure-induced amorphous structure is more thermally stable against crystallization.
High-pressure-quenched samples will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than otherwise comparable samples quenched at atmospheric pressure.
High-pressure-quenched samples will retain a higher amorphous fraction and show less crystallinity than atmospheric-pressure controls.
Conventionally quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys typically have lower glass-forming ability than high-pressure-quenched counterparts.
Conventionally quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys typically have lower amorphous-state thermal stability than high-pressure-quenched counterparts.
The beneficial effect requires pressure and cooling rate to exceed threshold values.
Pressures below approximately 2 GPa may be insufficient to suppress crystallization.
Very high pressures or other extreme processing conditions might induce alternative phase transformations.
